Winner: Andrew Brunette's job security
After the Nashville Predators missed the playoffs in two straight seasons and the team hired a new general manager in Chris MacFarland, the future of head coach Andrew Brunette seemed murky at best.

He appears safe for now: Nashville has been one of the league's bigger surprises through 18 games, going 9-4-5 and sitting in a Western Conference playoff spot.

Yes, the Predators are extremely top-heavy, as their veteran stars are carrying the offense. But rebound seasons from Juuse Saros and Roman Josi have helped make Nashville a playoff contender and keep their coach off the hot seat.

Loser: Jeff Blashill's job security
The Chicago Blackhawks are terrible (again), which has led the widespread speculation that Blashill probably will lose his job. But GM Kyle Davidson said Blashill is "our head coach" and "I have full confidence in him."

So there you go: Jeff Blashill is the head coach of the Chicago Blackhawks. That should end the speculation, as all votes of confidence from general managers do.

Winner: 'Expected win probability'
Whether or not it was the actual rationale for not playing Connor Hellebuyck against his former team the Winnipeg Jets on Tuesday, the New Jersey Devils are now permanently married to the phrase "a reduction in our expected win probability."

The Jets clowned the Devils about it online and in the arena, where the scoreboard said New Jersey's win probability was 0% after their 4-2 loss.

Every Devils' loss, going forward? "Expected win probability" memes. Every Devils' playoff elimination? "Expected win probability" memes. The unintended consequences of diversionary tactics.

Loser: Connor Hellebuyck's approach
As I've previously reported, it's my understanding that Hellebuyck's primary motivation to ask out of Winnipeg was hockey-related, although his news conference Tuesday was focused primarily on the threats and abuse that he said his family received after Hellebuyck won Olympic gold for the United States and attended the State of the Union address.

With the benefit of hindsight, I think he would have been better off focusing on "the uncertainty with my career," as he briefly phrased it. Being 33 years old, wanting to win a Stanley Cup, seeing the Jets miss the playoffs and have talent defections like Nikolaj Ehlers in the past two seasons ... I can't help but feel that would have been more well-received by some fans, especially given how much he gave the organization (three Vezinas and a Hart).

Winner: Cutter Gauthier
He had 15 goals through his first 17 games for the Ducks, who continue to be the NHL's wildest ride (3.83 goals for, 3.67 goals against per game).

All of this is happening while the team he rejected -- the Philadelphia Flyers -- are again faced with the possibility of trading a young offensive star who doesn't want to be there.

Loser: Jakob Chychrun's follower count
The NHL Follow Tracker account on X, which monitors the Instagram activity of NHL players, continues to serve up the occasional juicy gossip nugget. Like Ottawa Senators forward Nick Cousins unfollowing Washington Capitals defenseman Jakob Chychrun, with whom he was teammates during their time in Arizona.

This came after Chychrun delivered one of the hardest legal checks in recent NHL history to put Cousins out of their game Tuesday night -- a hit that impacted Cousins to the point where he unfollowed Chychrun's IG account at 2:48 a.m., according to the tracker. Obviously, Cousins has decided making this statement is more important than more videos of shirtless defensemen eating whole watermelons.

FAVORITE ON-ICE MOMENT

The only opportunity Jets fans had to share their feelings with Hellebuyck was when he skated out for warmups with the Devils. The crowd reacted every time the maligned goalie had a puck fly past him. So his New Jersey teammates serve him up some absolute muffins for easy saves, to deprive them of their chance to jeer.

FAVORITE OFF-ICE MOMENT
I greatly anticipated Hellebuyck's return to Winnipeg because Jets fans are viciously creative in their arena chanting when properly motivated. I still remember them chanting "silver medal!" at Ryan Miller 14 years ago, referencing his Olympic gold medal game loss in 2010.

They did not disappoint in Hellebuyck's return to Winnipeg. Mike McIntrye of the Winnipeg News chronicled the chants Tuesday night. Here's my Anti-Hellebuyck Chant Power Rankings:

5. WHERE IS CONNOR? (Calling out Hellebuyck as he didn't start and didn't even sit near the ice as a backup.)

4. F--- YOU HELLY (Straight and to the point, although not exactly Manitoba Nice.)

3. PLAYOFF CHOKER (Attacking both his legacy and his mental toughness. Well done.)

2. YOU'RE A COWARD, HELLEBUYCK, sung to tune of Oh My Darling, Clementine (No notes. Perfect.)

1. YOU CAN'T FISH HERE (Hellebuyck is one of the NHL's most prolific fishermen, to the point where he referenced it in his recent Instagram statement before even mentioning his former Jets teammates. To close him off from the beautiful Canadian lakes and their bounty of aquatic life ... not doubt these words hurt the most.)

MUST-SEE GAMES

Washington Capitals at New Jersey Devils

Nov. 12, 7 p.m. ET

The Devils claimed that Hellebuyck didn't face the Jets because they wanted him rested and ready for a home and home against the division rival Capitals. Imagine, for a moment, that he doesn't play well in these games? Yikes.

Edmonton Oilers at Florida Panthers

Nov. 17, 7 p.m. ET

Animosity still runs deep between these two, who met for the Stanley Cup in back-to-back seasons (2024-25). But from an Oilers' perspective, this will be a solid early test for a team that has been one of the NHL's best so far.

PUCK HEADLINES
DATELINE: Philadelphia
ESPN's Kevin Weekes dropped a bombshell Tuesday night with a report that Flyers star winger Matvei Michkov "wanted a new start elsewhere," and that there was internal turmoil between him and the team, and would be a prime trade candidate. There was pushback from coach Rick Tocchet and GM Daniel Briere that Michkov had not asked for a trade, with Briere calling Weekes' report "not correct."

Of course, Weekes never reported that Michkov had demanded a trade. But nonetheless ...

Briere had media availability Wednesday night to address the report and dispel any notion that Michkov or his representatives had expressed a desire to have him traded. "What was told to us was that they were not behind it," the Flyers' GM said.

What Briere didn't do was dispel the notion that there's friction between Michkov and his teammates. He was asked about the "internal turmoil" that Weekes cited and speculation about a rift between teammates, as was potentially evidenced by a public spat on the bench between Michkov and defenseman Nick Seeler recently.

"There's always moments. It's like brothers and sisters fighting. It happens. We saw it the other night on the bench with Nick Seeler," he said. "They're competitive guys. Matvei is one of the most competitive players that we've had here in a while. And when you're not winning, yeah, there's some rifts here or there. I've been through it in my career many, many times."

So yes, there is turmoil between Michkov and his teammates. Briere says he believes it can be chalked up to the Flyers' stumble this season.

"I'm actually glad that they don't accept it. And if they were all good with what's happening, I'd be more worried," he said.

DATELINE: GM meetings
NHL commissioner Gary Bettman is still monitoring player use of no-trade clauses to force movement to the teams of their choosing.

"If it's a problem, and one offseason does not a problem make, we'll have to address it with the Players Association," he said in Toronto this week. "My view is that a no-trade clause is not a one-way street and a player isn't entitled to be traded if his team doesn't want to trade him."

We've heard that from Bettman before, but he added something in his post-GM meetings news conference: "A player is not entitled to demand a trade under contract. Contracts have meaning."

I disagree. Players are entitled to demand a trade while under contract. They're just not entitled to be traded wherever they choose, which has been the issue with the no-trade clauses.

Look at a situation like the Dylan Larkin drama in Detroit. Interim GM Shawn Horcoff says he believes there are trades he can make if Larkin expands his trade list. Larkin probably believes that he'll end up in a place where he wants to be -- like Minnesota -- if he just sticks to his current list and waits out the Wings.

He can't trade himself. That's up to Detroit. It's just a matter of who blinks first. In almost every situation we've seen in the player empowerment era, it's the team that does. Which is why Bettman is having to pay this any mind.

stories.headline: F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?
stories.summary: The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.
stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - TBC

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal runs until the end of the 2026 season, and he said a decision on his future will come later in the year. At 45 years old, the decision is likely to be between continuing with an underperforming Aston Martin team, or calling time on his F1 career once and for all.

Lance Stroll - TBC

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026, although his position for 2027 has not formally been confirmed.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Rafael Câmara - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2027

F2 star Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon for the 2027 season on a multi-year agreement. The reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader will make his debut in F1 and will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. The exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - 2027

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat was only confirmed for the current season, but the New Zealander has proved his case after a series of strong performances, meaning he has now secured his seat for the 2027 season.

Arvid Lindblad - 2027

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie was only confirmed for this season, but will now partner alongside Lawson for 2027.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2029

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with newcomers Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement and has now extended his contract which will see him stay with the American team until 2029.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Valtteri Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: UFC's Josh Hokit says he'll 'never' regret vulgar Michelle Obama remarks
stories.summary: UFC fighter Josh Hokit, who will challenger for the heavyweight title on Saturday, says he'll "never" regret his vulgar comments about former First Lady Michelle Obama,
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- UFC heavyweight Josh Hokit said he has no regrets about using the White House as a bully pulpit to make an extraordinary and unfounded attack based on a right-wing conspiracy theory about former first lady Michelle Obama.

Hokit made his vulgar remarks inside the Octagon in June after winning his fight at the UFC event to mark President Donald Trump's 80th birthday on the South Lawn of the White House.

Hokit fights for the first time since then on Saturday when he challenges heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane in the main event of UFC 334 at Madison Square Garden.

Hokit again made a series of crass insults about other fighters on the fight card on Wednesday inside a New York hotel before taking questions about his championship bout and his remarks on Obama.

"I'll never look back and be like, I regret that," Hokit said.

Wearing a black stocking cap over an American flag bandana, sunglasses and fight gloves, Hokit said he "took the rap of a villain" before he burst into what he called a freestyle rap to express his lack of regret.

Hokit said he was "sure it wasn't" the right thing to do to insult the former first lady but was proud the remarks had put his image on Trump's Truth Social posts. In one post, Hokit appeared in cartoon form alongside UFC chief Dana White in the White House briefing room.

Trump said over the weekend he had offered White the job of White House press secretary. White declined the frivolous offer.

"I'm here to take what's mine," Hokit said. "If I've got to rub some people the wrong way, if I've got to say some (stuff) in the wrong location, it is what it is. Was it not a good location to say it? I mean, we're at the White House. That house represents freedom of speech. So it is what it is. I think it was the perfect location to say it."

The 28-year-old Hokit is 10-0 in his MMA career and has won all six fights since joining UFC in 2025.

stories.headline: AFL Draft: Key dates, FAQs, players to know, and more
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL draft is rapidly approaching, so here's your guide for what to know, including key dates and times, players to know, academy-linked names, and every club's pick.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is fast approaching. Marvel Stadium will once more play host to the first round at 7:00pm AEDT on November 19, with the draft recommencing for the second round onwards on November 20.

Key dates and times
Where: Marvel Stadium

How to watch: Fox Footy

First round: Thursday, November 19, 7pm AEDT

Second round onwards: Friday, November 20, 7pm AEDT

Preseason and rookie draft: Monday, November 23, 3pm AEDT

Each club's picks

*As at Nov. 11
Adelaide: 15, 32, 35, 43, 54

Brisbane: 21, 27, 28, 45

Carlton: 13, 18, 31, 50, 59, 67, 73

Collingwood: 11, 30, 63, 64, 65

Essendon: 1, 17, 25, 69, 75, 78, 80 (plus second round compensation pick)

Fremantle: 19, 40, 58, 61, 68

Geelong: 36, 55, 60

Gold Coast: 8, 70, 72, 77

GWS: 9, 20, 26, 57

Hawthorn: 29, 37, 66, 74

Melbourne: 4, 14, 48, 51, 79

North Melbourne: 33, 49, 62

Port Adelaide: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46

Richmond: 2, 5, 44, 76 (plus second round compensation pick)

St Kilda: 10, 16, 41

Sydney: 6, 38, 39, 47

West Coast: 3, 23, 56 (plus second round compensation pick)

Western Bulldogs: 42, 52, 53, 71

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: Ex-San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu files fair housing lawsuit
stories.summary: Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court.
stories.body:
Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court against one real estate firm, two property owners and two real estate agents, according to information contained in the filing.

The lawsuit, a copy of which has been viewed by ESPN, alleges the defendants discriminated against Bakambu and his wife, Anne-Laure Hueber, on the basis of "familial status" by denying them the opportunity rent a house because they had children who would be living with them.

According to the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, the individuals and entities listed as defendants are property owners JW Wealth and Sheila Nasehi, real estate firm Compass California III and Compass agents Gillian Gillies and Bree Bornstein.

Neither Major League Soccer nor San Diego FC are named as a defendant in the lawsuit.

Bakambu and Hueber are seeking unspecified compensatory, statutory and punitive damages, as well as declaratory and injunctive relief, attorney's fees and costs under the Fair Housing Act, the California Fair Employment and Housing Act and the Unruh Civil Rights Act.

Bakambu signed with San Diego FC back on Sept. 3, and in nine matches for SDFC, he scored four goals with one assist.

In an Instagram post dated Nov. 6, Bakambu, a Congo DR international who played at last summer's World Cup, announced that he would no longer be playing for San Diego, stating, "Some decisions are beyond our control."

A request for comment from a representative for JW Wealth wasn't successful. A request for comment from Compass was also not successful.

ESPN has asked San Diego FC and the league for comment. the MLS players' association declined an ESPN request for comment.

The suit, which was filed on Monday, alleged two instances of discrimination. In the first alleged incident, Bakambu made an offer to rent a 5,679 square-foot house in San Diego, Calif. for a monthly rent of $17,500.

The filing details how Gillies, the agent representing Compass, stated that a pool barrier "would be required due to the age of the children" and asked whether Bakambu would pay an estimated $6,000 to install it if the owner approved.

Alternatives were proposed by Bakambu's broker, Sandra Shebani, including mesh covers and splash alarms.

Gillies responded: "A barrier will need to be installed."

The requirement wasn't mentioned in the property listing.

By Sept. 16, Bakambu made an updated offer that included paying a year's rent in advance, a Pool and Spa Liability Addendum, and an agreement to pay for the barrier.

According to the filing, Compass managing director Melanie Fontana later told Shebani that another applicant that met the lease requirements was under consideration, that Bakambu's offer had been received and that the owner would fund any pool safety measures.

The lawsuit goes on to state that on Sept. 18, 2026, Ms. Shebani raised the fair-housing concern directly with Kathy Mehringer, Compass's Broker of Record and Managing Director of Compliance and Risk Management.

Mehringer responded: "Melanie has explained the process. Compass is not violating any fair housing rules - why would you accuse us of doing so? That is not collaboration."

The filing states that Bakambu's offer was never accepted, and the rental listing was withdrawn from the market after his real estate agent raised fair-housing concerns with Compass management. The suit states that by tying rental conditions to the children and their ages, Bakambu and Hueber were discriminated against.

Later, Bakambu and Hueber sought to rent a 6,300 square-foot house through Compass in Rancho Santa Fe, Calif., and on Oct. 11, 2026, after viewing the property with Bornstein, offered a monthly rent of $23,500.

The filing states: "The offer and follow-up from Ms. Hueber went unanswered even after Plaintiffs observed the home being advertised for $20,000 per month by October 26, 2026."

On Nov. 6, the rental property was taken off the market.

The suit alleges that Compass and Bornstein, its listing agent for the second property, discriminated against Bakambu and Hueber by failing to consider or negotiate their offer because of familial status, and that this was in retaliation for Bakambu and Hueber raising fair-housing concerns regarding negotiations for the first property.

While this was going on, Bakambu's family was forced to remain in temporary housing at his own expense, according to the filing.

The filing reads: "Cédric and Anne allege that this sequence was not [an] ordinary rental negotiation. They were denied equal consideration because their household included five children, and Compass subjected them to further adverse treatment after they asserted their fair-housing rights.

"The consequences were concrete: lost housing opportunities, additional expenses, prolonged housing instability, disruption of efforts to arrange schooling and activities for their children, humiliation, and emotional distress."

stories.headline: How the Atlanta Dream turned their franchise around in just five years
stories.summary: Five years ago, the Dream were the second-worst team in the WNBA -- making their Finals run all the more remarkable.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Just five years ago, the idea of the Atlanta Dream competing for the WNBA championship trophy would have seemed as unlikely as a rebound landing untouched next to Angel Reese.

So finishing within one victory of a title, as the Dream did in the WNBA Finals last week, says a lot about just how far the franchise has come since 2021. Even without the 2026 championship, what the Dream did in revitalizing their franchise is a story that shouldn't be lost in Golden State's celebration. Five years ago, the Dream were a mess. Now, they're contenders. That's something other WNBA franchises can look to.

"It's remarkable, really," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Consider how far the franchise was from this in 2021.

That was the year the Dream moved to Gateway Center Arena -- the smallest venue in the WNBA at 3,500 seats -- because too much of their longtime larger home (State Farm Arena, capacity 17,608) was vacant during games. The Dream had three different coaches that year, one resigning just before the season began to take a college job. Chennedy Carter, their lottery-pick selection from 2020, was suspended in July and never returned. They finished in second-to-last place in the WNBA at 8-24.

The team's most notable moment came not on court, but in a viral video of two Dream players throwing punches by a food truck outside an Atlanta nightclub.

Those were the low points. But behind the scenes, two big moves in 2021 helped spark a turnaround: an ownership change, led by real estate investor Larry Gottesdiener, and a new general manager, Dan Padover.

Reese was then a college sophomore with huge goals for her future. But it wasn't until this April that she knew those plans would intersect with the Dream.

"When I play with joy and I'm surrounded by people that just genuinely make me happy, I think I'm at my best," Reese said. "The organization has poured into me. To be in my third year [in the WNBA], this is obviously the best situation I've ever been in."

And even as Reese and teammates Jordin Canada and Allisha Gray sat somberly in the Dream's postgame news conference after Game 7, the joyful sounds of Ballhalla's celebration audible, they looked dissatisfied but not devastated.

"They changed my life," Reese said of the Atlanta players and staff. "And I'm just so grateful for them."

A 2008 EXPANSION TEAM, the Dream's first title hopes were led by another Angel -- 2009 No. 1 pick Angel McCoughtry. She led the Dream to the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but they were swept each time.

The Dream then missed the playoffs six of the next nine years. They won a then-franchise record 23 games in 2018, but lost McCoughtry to a knee injury Aug. 7 and lost 3-2 in the semifinals.

Without McCoughtry in 2019, the Dream averaged just 4,270 fans for home games, necessitating the move from State Farm Arena. That relocation was delayed a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the 2020 season was in a "bubble" in Bradenton, Florida. By then, McCoughtry had left in free agency for Las Vegas.

The Dream's leadership became a focus for all WNBA players in the bubble when co-owner Kelly Loeffler sent a letter to commissioner Cathy Engelbert opposing the league's decision to display "Black Lives Matter" logos on the courts in Bradenton. Loeffler wrote "we need less -- not more -- politics in sports."

Loeffler was involved in a political race at the time, seeking to hold her U.S. Senate seat. The divide mushroomed into WNBA players campaigning for her opponent, Raphael Warnock.

"Being on the outside of the Dream looking in then, during that time everybody was rallying around them," said guard Jordin Canada, then with the Seattle Storm, of the bubble activism against Loeffler's continued ownership. "We wanted what was best for them and the W as a whole, and to see that transition into a more positive direction."

The situation was untenable, and the franchise was sold in February 2021 to Gottesdiener's group, which included former WNBA player Renee Montgomery.

"I believed the WNBA was an extraordinary opportunity, not just to grow the game of basketball," Gottesdiener said, "but to demonstrate what's possible when you invest in women."

Padover, who joined the Dream in October 2021, had worked for the Las Vegas Aces for three years, helping build the team that would become a three-time champion. He went from a franchise a step from the top to one with nowhere to go but up.

Padover started his WNBA career as a video coordinator with the New York Liberty in 2012, and he has credited former coach and GM Bill Laimbeer for helping him develop into a team executive. He cites this key from Laimbeer.

"If you can get your organization organized and you can take care of the players, you can start to establish yourself as a place that is respected," Padover said. "Under previous ownership, I think we were disorganized, and we didn't really have an identity.

"When I got here the goal was, 'Let's turn Atlanta back into a franchise that's respected throughout the WNBA community, one piece at a time, and that will allow us to be able to build something.' We started with things like player housing, staffing, and medical and player development."

THE OTHER PIECE was putting the right players and coaches in the building. Padover, who has been named the league's executive of the year three times, put his trade wizardry to use. He dealt the Nos. 3 and 14 picks in the 2022 draft and a 2023 pick swap to Washington for the No. 1 pick in 2022 to select Rhyne Howard.

"It was a huge boost of confidence," Howard said. "Obviously, when you get drafted, that means the team wants you. But to do it in the way that they did -- trading up to get me like that -- put no doubt in my mind that I was a piece that they were looking for to start this new journey, to start this new outcome that we're having."

The 6-foot-2 guard was Rookie of the Year and has since been a four-time All-Star. She averaged 17.7 points in the regular season this year and 16.3 in the playoffs. Howard won't recall Game 7 fondly -- she was limited to six points on 3-of-14 shooting -- but she took noticeable steps forward as a player in 2026, especially on defense.

Padover also got the steal of the second round in 2022 with forward Naz Hillmon, who became a full-time starter this season and has played more WNBA games than anyone from that draft class.

Subsequent huge deals came for guards Gray (2023) and Canada (2024).

"One of the things that I definitely took from Bill was not to be skittish to give up things in trades," Padover said. "If you're doing it to get a great player, it's always worth it, and don't be afraid to do that."

One of Padover's biggest moves in 2025 was bringing in Smesko, who had spent most of his career as a college coach, including 17 years at Florida Gulf Coast.

"Obviously, there was a changing landscape in college basketball, and I was at the point where a new challenge was needed," Smesko said of his decision to move to the WNBA. "It was Atlanta, and I love the city. And I thought there was the makings of a core that could compete for a championship."

Atlanta went 30-14 last season but lost in the first round of the playoffs. Padover used a trade to acquire the last key component. On April 6, the Dream obtained Reese from the Chicago Sky for future draft picks. Reese had become disillusioned with the Sky's direction and voiced her concerns near the end of the 2025 season. She believed in the Dream's vision, just as the players obtained before her did.

"I feel like the organization has gotten to a point where players want to come play for Atlanta," Gray said. "To be able to get Angel just speaks volumes of how the organization is run and how it really cares for players. The city of Atlanta is great. Great culture. The games just feel like one big family cookout, and everybody's welcome."

Reese proved to be the final and most essential ingredient. Other than a five-game skid June 24-July 4, the Dream -- who also added veteran DeWanna Bonner late in the season -- stayed consistent, finishing 30-14 again. Reese had the best offensive year of her career, averaging 16.4 points, plus 12.1 rebounds.

"She's made me look good all season long," Howard said. "And I'm sure she's going to continue to do that for the rest of her time here. Shoutout to her for coming in and being bought in. She's handled every challenge that we've thrown at her with grace."

This year's Finals games in Atlanta didn't come without hurdles -- facility conflicts with State Farm Arena meant one Finals game had to be moved up a day and another had to be played at 12:30 p.m. ET on a Thursday. But even that early game was joyful and loud, a full house of fans skipping work and school to cheer on the Dream in a must-win Game 6.

Next year, the Dream moves back to State Farm Arena full time, playing all 25 regular-season home games there.

And as disappointed as the Dream were after losing Game 7, they also immediately expressed excitement about the 2027 season.

"Just because we didn't win today doesn't mean that we won't be champions in the future," Reese said.

Those words weren't just platitudes after a disappointing ending. Next year, with every starter already signed to return, the Dream could at last win that elusive title.

"I like our chemistry and just the sisterhood that we have as a team," said Gray, who played every Finals game despite sustaining an injury on her shooting hand in the semifinals. "We actually love each other and enjoy being around each other."

stories.headline: 'Confident': Perth Bears upbeat about signing Burton
stories.summary: Fresh off unveiling their new away jumper, the Perth Bears are confident of securing Canterbury and Origin star Matt Burton for their NRL entry.
stories.body:
The Perth Bears are optimistic of securing Matt Burton's signature within days, in a huge boost to the NRL's expansion club.

General manager Gareth Holmes took the opportunity to spruik the club's chances of snaring the Test and NSW State of Origin star at Thursday's unveiling of the side's away jumper at North Sydney Oval.

The Bears, albeit playing mostly out of Western Australia, will emerge from 28 years in hibernation when they rejoin the NRL in 2027.

And Holmes is confident Burton will be on deck for the side's round-one clash after the Canterbury utility scouted the club's facilities this week.

"It's no secret he spent the weekend in Perth with his family," Holmes said.

"He got to see what a wonderful place Perth is. The weather turned out for him, he got to experience it, he got to catch up with a few familiar faces and former teammates there, so I think he really enjoyed himself.

"We're really keen to have him and so over the next week or so I hope that we have a bit more news about that.

"I've got to be confident. We presented something to him in terms of being part of a team that is new and the desire for him to play six is there as well."

Holmes believes Burton reuniting with his former Bulldogs halves partner Toby Sexton would be a boon for the Bears.

"Matt's got some decisions to make, and they're big ones, but he understands what he's coming to and it's an exciting time for him, whichever way he goes," Holmes said.

In a major boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys in August granted the Bears a concession for signing a marquee player.

The club will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for recruiting any player on a salary above $1 million.

The move effectively means they could sign a marquee player such as Burton, or potentially Sam Walker, for, say, $1.8 million a season, but any third-party sponsor's input of $300,000 would not be counted in the NRL salary cap.

Despite the concessions, the Bears have been unable to secure any real big names.

Melbourne pair Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, Penrith premiership winners Scott Sorensen and Liam Henry, Sexton and Canberra hardman Corey Horsburgh have been the biggest recruits.

The signings pale into comparison to the PNG Chiefs, who have used the NRL's tax-free incentives to lure the likes of representative superstars Jarome Luai, Brian To'o, Joey Manu, Zac Lomax, Connor Watson and the league's greatest ever tryscorer Alex Johnston for their 2028 entry.

Asked if the Bears were on a level recruitment playing field with the Chiefs, one-club legend Billy Moore said: "Like North Sydney, there's no excuses", while Holmes said the 20 per cent dispensation "helps".

Perth are also hoping to stage a trial match at North Sydney Oval in late February, despite pushback from Cricket NSW.

Cricket NSW told the Bears it would cost around $200,000 to relocate Sydney grade games and the NRL club would need to foot the bill.

"It's above my pay grade," said Moore, believing that returning to the club's spiritual home to reconnect with old fans was vital.

"But $200,000, get a GoFundMe page going if need be."

It is understood discussions between the two parties are continuing.
